title: The empty gas tank that was not empty and became Teflon
hook: A gas tank that looked empty gave us Teflon.
summary: In 1938 DuPont chemist Roy Plunkett found a gas cylinder that was heavy but would not release gas; inside was PTFE, Teflon, later used in the Manhattan Project and then on frying pans.
sources: Wikipedia: Polytetrafluoroethylene and Roy J. Plunkett: discovered April 1938 at DuPont's Jackson Laboratory; a tetrafluoroethylene cylinder would not release gas but weighed as if full; cut open, waxy slippery white powder found.
Science History Institute: Roy Plunkett and the discovery of Teflon; use of PTFE in Manhattan Project seals and gaskets, later cookware.

lines.text: A gas tank that looked empty gave us Teflon.
lines.caps: A gas *tank | that looked *empty | gave us *Teflon

lines.text: In nineteen thirty-eight, chemist Roy Plunkett opened a valve, and no gas came out.
lines.caps: In *1938, | chemist Roy *Plunkett | opened a *valve, | and no *gas came out

lines.text: But the tank weighed as much as a full one, so he cut it open.
lines.caps: But it *weighed | as *much as | a *full one, | so he *cut it open

image.search: DuPont Jackson Laboratory Deepwater New Jersey

lines.text: Inside was a slippery white powder, a brand new plastic.
lines.caps: Inside was a *slippery | white *powder, | a brand new *plastic

lines.text: Almost nothing could stick to it, and chemicals could not eat it.
lines.caps: Almost *nothing | *could stick to it, | and *chemicals | *could not eat it

lines.text: That made it perfect for the Manhattan Project's pipes and seals.
Only later did it coat frying pans, all because he weighed an empty tank.
lines.caps: Only *later, | *frying pans, | all because he *weighed | an empty *tank

post.caption:
A heavy tank that gave out no gas changed every kitchen.
Would you have cut the tank open, or thrown it away?
Follow @unt.oldfiles for a new untold story every day.
